what_it_does: Running large language models on CPU servers equipped with high-bandwidth memory chips (HBM — a type of fast, stacked memory) is severely slowed not by the memory or the math hardware, but by the software code that converts compressed model weights back into a usable format before each computation step. DECA is a small hardware unit placed next to each CPU core that takes over this decompression work, freeing the CPU's vector math units to stay idle and letting memory and matrix hardware run at their full speed.
method_in_detail:
The diagnosis. Intel's recent server CPUs include a matrix multiplication unit (TMUL — similar in purpose to a GPU's tensor cores, the dedicated hardware blocks for large matrix math) that is extremely fast, and HBM that supplies data quickly. But when model weights are stored in compressed form — either as low-bit floating-point numbers (4-bit or 8-bit instead of 16-bit) or with many zeros removed to save space (sparsification) — the CPU must first run many vector (AVX) instructions to decode them back into the format TMUL accepts. Profiling shows these decoding instructions consume over 95% of the CPU's instruction slots, completely overwhelming the vector units and leaving the fast matrix hardware mostly idle.

The new analytical model. The authors extend the classic 'roofline' model (which only considers memory bandwidth and compute throughput) into a three-dimensional 'Roof-Surface' that adds a third axis: how many vector operations are needed per matrix operation. This model correctly predicts that highly compressed workloads are bottlenecked by vector throughput, not memory or matrix compute — something the 2D roofline misses entirely. It also shows that simply adding 4x more vector units to the CPU would not fix the problem, because the CPU's instruction pipeline itself is already nearly full.

DECA's design. DECA sits next to the L2 cache, connected to each CPU core through a small shared interface. Its internal pipeline has three stages: (1) Dequantization: a parallel lookup table array (each table has 256 entries, one per possible low-bit value) converts compressed integers back to 16-bit floats — multiple values in parallel per cycle. (2) Expansion: a crossbar (a hardware switching network) inserts zeros back at the positions indicated by a bitmask, reconstructing the dense tile from the sparse nonzero array. Position indices are computed on-the-fly by a parallel prefix-sum circuit. (3) Scaling: per-group scale factors are applied. Two copies of the load buffers and output registers allow DECA to be loading and decompressing one tile while the CPU is consuming the previous tile — classic hardware double buffering.

The key ISA extension. If the CPU communicates with DECA using ordinary memory operations, every iteration requires a memory fence (a full stop that prevents later instructions from starting until earlier ones finish), serializing everything. DECA introduces a new instruction class called TEPL (Tile External Preprocess and Load) that behaves like a speculative load: the CPU issues it early and out of order, DECA starts decompressing immediately, and the result appears in a CPU tile register when the instruction finally 'completes.' If the CPU needs to roll back (branch misprediction, etc.), it sends a squash signal and DECA aborts cleanly, since DECA never modifies memory.

The result. Using the Roof-Surface model to size DECA optimally (32-element output width, 8 parallel lookup tables), and adding TEPL, DECA achieves up to 4x speedup over the Intel software-only baseline for compressed matrix multiplications on an HBM server, and reduces full model inference time for Llama2-70B by 1.6–2.6x — all with a hardware area overhead of less than 0.2% of the chip.
